title: The Nirmalas
hook: scholars who, tradition says, were sent to study Sanskrit learning in Benares

segments.voice: Yesterday, Udasi places today: deras and akharas in Punjab and beyond. Your line was still standing. Which old place on your route did you notice? Day one thousand three hundred five.

Why would a Guru send his Sikhs away to study under teachers of another tradition? Follow the road east, toward the holy city on the Ganges. A few young Sikhs are walking it with bundles on their backs, heading for teachers who may never have taught a Sikh before. They'll sit on the floor with students of another tradition, learn a difficult old language, memorize grammar until their heads ache, and read books in a script that's new to them. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh sent them. The order that traces itself to those students is today's word.
screen: `A ROAD EAST, TO THE GANGES.` → `STUDENTS FROM ANOTHER TRADITION.` → `WHY WOULD A GURU SEND THEM?`

segments.voice: The story first, as tradition tells it. Guru Gobind Singh wanted Sikhs who could read the learning of the classical Indian schools for themselves: Sanskrit grammar, philosophy, the old texts that learned men of his day quoted in their arguments. So, tradition says, he sent a small band of Sikhs to Benares, the city on the Ganges known for that learning, to study. They came back as scholars, and the Nirmalas trace their order to them. Some accounts add details: names, a disguise, a teacher who at first refused them. The accounts differ, so today keeps only the shape. Second, the name. Nirmal is a word the Gurus use in their hymns. It means spotless, pure, without stain, and they say it of the Name, of the mind made clear, of God. An order of scholars called itself by that word, the pure ones. Third, what learning is for. Guru Nanak has a short line in Raag Asa that the Nirmalas could have carried as their motto. In paraphrase: when learning is reflected upon, it becomes a kindness to others. Not learning to win arguments. Not learning to stand above people. Learning thought through until it can help someone. Fourth, what they became. Nirmalas are remembered as teachers and preachers who explained the Gurus' hymns, drawing on the language of the scholars of their day. Some Sikhs value that bridge; some ask how much the borrowed language shaped the reading. Both questions are fair, and tomorrow looks at the explaining itself. So here's the picture: a Guru who thought study was worth a long walk, and an order named for a spotless one.
screen: `TRADITION: SENT TO BENARES TO STUDY.` · `NIRMAL: SPOTLESS, WITHOUT STAIN.` · `LEARNING THAT HELPS OTHERS.` · `A BRIDGE, AND A FAIR QUESTION.` · then, large: `THE SCHOLARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: study one hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Choose something you've been avoiding because it's difficult: a page you skipped, a skill you put down, a passage of scripture you never understood. Hold it in mind without trying to solve it. Just let it sit there, in front of you, the way a student sits in front of a teacher. Breathe in: I don't know this yet. Breathe out: I can begin. After the bell, give it ten honest minutes. The bell holds the time.
Nirmala. The pure ones: an order of Sikh scholars who, tradition says, trace themselves to students Guru Gobind Singh sent to Benares. Today's word.
Your line: the scholars. Today, when you learn one new thing, pass it on to one person who could use it. Learning thought through becomes a kindness. Day one thousand three hundred five.
